context_blurb:
Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, explained how living things change over generations. Breeders change them by choosing which ones breed: artificial selection. In the wild, those whose inherited traits best suit their surroundings leave the most young, so those traits spread: natural selection, as Darwin named it. It is settled science, and it can be watched at work.

In the Origin's fifth edition, Darwin adopted Herbert Spencer's phrase survival of the fittest, but to a biologist fitness means how many young an animal leaves, not its strength or speed. Among four stags in a wood, the fittest is the one that fathers the most fawns; a champion fighter that fathers none passes on nothing.

Darwin joined two pigeon clubs in London and kept every breed he could get, among them the fantail, fanning thirty or forty tail feathers where most pigeons carry twelve or fourteen. Fanciers believed each main breed had its own wild ancestor. Darwin concluded instead that all the breeds came from one wild species, the rock pigeon, reshaped by breeders choosing which birds to mate.

From wild cabbage, farmers chose big leaves for kale, the big tip bud for cabbage and the side buds for Brussels sprouts. Picking the plants whose flower buds grew in the biggest bunches gave broccoli, a crowd of unopened buds on thick stalks. All remain one species.

Teosinte, the wild Mexican grass that became corn, bears a dozen kernels at most per little ear, each locked in a stony case. A one-gene change leaves a kernel bare; it arose by chance, and no farmer could cause it. By planting seed from the plants with the change, season after season, farmers in southwestern Mexico made it common, starting about 9,000 years ago.

Selection can only choose among differences that already exist. For generations rose growers kept their bluest seedlings, yet got nothing bluer than lilac or purple. No rose has the gene needed to make delphinidin, the blue pigment of pansies, so there was no blue to choose. A bluish rose came later only by genetic engineering, with a pansy gene, and even it is lavender-mauve.

Robert Wayne's DNA studies in the 1990s showed that dogs descend from wolves, and every breed, from the Chihuahua to the Great Dane, was shaped from them by people's choosing. A breeder who allows only her tiniest dogs to have puppies is doing artificial selection, since a person chose the parents. Among strays in a hot city, where short coats survive better, the heat, not a person, decides which dogs breed: natural selection, though people built the city.

Each dose of an antibiotic kills the bacteria it can, and the few that resist it live and multiply, passing their resistance on, so an infection can come back resistant. No bacterium learns to resist, and a patient's body never becomes resistant, though three people in four believed it did in a 2015 survey.

Spraying with DDT, an insect-killing chemical, spread in the 1940s, and by 1947 houseflies in Europe were shrugging it off. Selection works one generation at a time, and a housefly can grow from egg to adult in about ten days, so flies pass through ten or more generations a year.

The peppered moth's dark form was rare until factory soot blackened England's woods; by 1895 it made up about 98 in 100 near Manchester. In 1953 Bernard Kettlewell released paint-marked pale and dark moths in a sooty wood near Birmingham and recaptured about twice the share of dark ones as of pale. In a clean Dorset wood with lichen-pale bark, he got back two to three times as many pale moths as dark. With no soot to blame and the result reversed, the cause was camouflage: matching the bark kept a moth alive, because birds hunting by sight, filmed by Niko Tinbergen, ate the moths that stood out.

Critics objected that Kettlewell's moths sat on bare trunks, packed more densely than in nature, so from 2001 to 2007 Michael Majerus re-ran the test in his garden outside Cambridge, setting twelve moths a night on branches, where the species usually rests, and watching for birds at dawn. Nine kinds of bird, robins and blue tits among them, took the dark moths more often than the pale, so Kettlewell's finding held up on the moths' natural resting sites. Published after his death, the work is the most direct evidence yet that camouflage and bird predation drive the change.
